Strategies are selected by in-loop scores and evaluated on held-out benchmarks. Across four tasks-math and code data selection, math reward design, and math curriculum learning-selected strategies achieve absolute gains over generic baselines of up to 13.34% on AIME25 Pass@32 and 5.85% averaged across four held-out benchmarks under fixed training conditions. In-loop scores improve over successive experiments, while held-out trajectories show that later in-loop gains do not always improve generalization. Comparisons of research organization and feedback access favor combining evidence analysis with cumulative findings. Research trajectories show how earlier findings inform strategy revisions and combinations across research directions.
  </details>

- **[Activation Steering with Jungian Cognitive Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20803)**  `arXiv:2607.20803`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI` `cs.LG`  
  _Liu Zai, Yumeng Wang, Junchen Fu, Suzan Verberne, Joemon M. Jose_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Controlling combinations of personality-related tendencies is important for adapting large language models to diverse interaction needs. But successful single-trait steering does not establish how to construct interventions for joint targets, or whether existing trait directions adequately represent them. We introduce a target-first framework that directly extracts steering directions from joint personality targets and then examines their decomposition into individual directions. To support this framework, we construct NarrationDB, linking character self-narrations to automatically evaluated joint scores across eight Jungian-inspired functions, a correspondence not directly available in existing Big Five- or MBTI-oriented resources. Experiments on three models demonstrate questionnaire-score controllability across the eight functions and coordinated changes in a tested two-function target. Directly extracted joint directions are better approximated by their corresponding individual directions than by unrelated pairings, but retain substantial residual components. Our work provides a method and resource for investigating joint personality control, with evidence that individual steering directions capture part, but not all, of the structure of joint targets.
  </details>

- **[Concurrency without Model Changes: Future-based Asynchronous Function Calling for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.15077)**  `arXiv:2605.15077`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI` `cs.LG`  
  _Guangyu Feng, Huanzhi Mao, Prabal Dutta, Joseph E. Gonzalez_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Function calling, also known as tool use, is a core capability of modern LLM agents but is typically constrained by synchronous execution semantics. Under these semantics, LLM decoding is blocked until each function call completes, resulting in increasing end-to-end latency. In this work, we introduce AsyncFC, a pure execution-layer framework that decouples LLM decoding from function execution, enabling overlap between model decoding and function execution as well as inter-function parallelism when dependencies permit. AsyncFC layers over existing models and unmodified function implementations, requiring no fine-tuning or changes to the standard synchronous function-calling protocol. On coding tasks, AsyncFC achieves a $1.4\times$ end-to-end speedup while preserving task accuracy. Furthermore, these results reveal that LLMs possess a native capability to reason over symbolic futures that represent unresolved execution results, enabling an asynchronous paradigm for model-tool interaction.
  </details>

- **[One Size Does Not Fit All: Distribution-Guided Tensor-Wise Adaptive Sparsification for Model Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.06163)**  `arXiv:2508.06163`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI` `cs.LG`  
  _Yingfeng Luo, Dingyang Lin, Junxin Wang, Kaiyan Chang, Ziqiang Xu, Weiqiao Shan, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Merging multiple task-specific fine-tuned checkpoints into a single multi-task model provides an attractive alternative to joint multi-task training. To mitigate cross-task interference, a common strategy is to sparsify task vectors before aggregation. However, many widely used methods rely on a uniform global sparsity ratio, overlooking differences in pruning sensitivity across tasks and parameter tensors. Consequently, such uniform sparsification may remove useful parameter updates from sensitive tensors while retaining redundant updates in others. To address this limitation, we propose TADrop, a plug-and-play sparsifier that independently determines tensor-specific keep ratios from their magnitude distributions using a scale-invariant quantile ratio. TADrop operates in a data-free manner by default, while offering optional lightweight module-level calibration when a small validation set is available. Experiments across vision, language, and multimodal benchmarks, including LLM and LoRA merging, demonstrate consistent improvements across multiple host merging methods, including a 4.99-point gain over EMR-Merging on RoBERTa GLUE. In many-task ViT-B/16 merging, the improvement increases with the number of tasks, reaching 2.26 points when merging 30 tasks. Further analyses show that TADrop preserves more task-associated neurons under matched overall sparsity. Together, these findings highlight the value of distribution-guided sparsification at the tensor level for improving model merging.
  </details>

- **[Open Foundation Models in Healthcare: Challenges, Paradoxes, and Opportunities with GenAI Driven Personalized Prescription](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04356)**  `arXiv:2502.04356`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI` `cs.LG`  
  _Mahdi Alkaeed, Sofiat Abioye, Adnan Qayyum, Yosra Magdi Mekki, Ilhem Berrou, Mohamed Abdallah, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In response to the success of proprietary Large Language Models (LLMs), there is a growing interest in developing open, non-proprietary LLMs and AI foundation models (AIFMs) for transparent use in academic, scientific, and non-commercial applications. Open models have substantial potential to improve healthcare applications. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive survey and a taxonomy of state-of-the-art open LLMs and AIFMs for clinical tasks. In addition, we empirically evaluate open-weight LLMs on a personalized-prescription task and compare them with a proprietary model with and without Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Across 100 synthetic patient profiles, the open-weight models matched or exceeded the proprietary baseline on overall suitability accuracy without retrieval augmentation (0.810--0.850 versus 0.780), although the confidence intervals overlap; with retrieval augmentation, every model improved, and the ranking closed to within 0.04. Gains from RAG were field-dependent rather than uniform. To highlight the clinical relevance of LLM-driven personalized prescriptions, we also conduct a subjective evaluation in which two raters, blinded to model and condition, scored responses independently of each other. Their ratings did not follow the accuracy gains: retrieval raised overall suitability accuracy for every model while lowering the two-rater means for two of the four on all five dimensions. Finally, we outline the ethical implications and potential risks associated with the misuse of advanced LLMs and AIFMs, highlighting the importance of responsible and transparent deployment in healthcare contexts. \textit{Data and code used in the paper will be released upon publication.
  </details>

- **[Tev: Scaling Long-Horizon Agentic Environments with Dense Progress Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18868)**  `arXiv:2610.18868`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI` `cs.CV` `cs.LG`  
  _Wenbo Hu, Shraman Pramanick, Krishna Kumar Singh, Nanyun Peng, Kai-Wei Chang, Yong Jae Lee_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Long-horizon agents have drawn growing attention for their ability to work autonomously -- from hours to days -- on economically valuable tasks, a capability essential to automated discovery and recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet open-source models still struggle on long-horizon tasks, largely for lack of both training data and a working recipe, and scaling both is hard: long, complex tasks are difficult to curate and verify, and their rewards are sparse. We address both. First, we introduce Tev-Gym, the first long-horizon agent training dataset with verifiable, dense, progressive rewards -- 1,170 verified task environments across 7 domains. It is built on a latent-world-first approach that first constructs a latent world: a complete and correct hidden specification of the task domain, workflow, and expected state after each step. Each task is then progressively rendered from this specification into an agent-facing environment, enabling controllable complexity and a natural progress metric. Second, we turn this metric into a training recipe: via progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS), we convert progress into a dense per-step reward that improves training efficiency and makes otherwise-intractable tasks trainable. Training with this recipe yields Tev-27B, which achieves substantial gains on the Agents' Last Exam computing and math sciences domains (ALE-CM), matching GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 at Pass@5. Despite training only on ALE-related data, it generalizes to the Terminal-Bench (TB) 3.0 and 4.0 subsets, surpassing GLM 5.2 and Gemini 3.7 Flash, and reaches Claude Opus 4.8-level performance on middle-horizon tasks such as TB 2.1.
  </details>

- **[Omni-Modal LLMs Know More Than They Say](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16135)**  `arXiv:2610.16135`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI` `cs.CV`  
  _Na Min An, Taekyung Kim, Jaemyung Yu, Hyunjung Shim, Dongyoon Han_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) extend LLMs to process heterogeneous modalities (e.g., vision, audio, and IMU signals) alongside language, enabling a broader range of multimodal tasks. Yet we find that these models often fail to express information from non-textual modalities even when they perceive it correctly. We term this disconnect knows-but-cannot-say. To investigate this phenomenon, we introduce Token-level Modality Alignment (TMA), which measures the alignment between individual modality representations and response representations. Our analysis shows that non-textual representations are less aligned with response tokens and receive less attention than textual representations, suggesting a potential explanation for uneven modality preferences. Motivated by these findings, we propose OmniCatalyst, a simple perceive $\rightarrow$ infer strategy that complements the original modality inputs with self-generated text, making non-textual knowledge more accessible. Across seven Omni-LLMs, OmniCatalyst consistently improves performance (+7.29%) and yields more balanced modality preferences, with further gains from diverse training strategies. Further analysis demonstrates that the knowledge extraction phases increase TMA, suggesting that improved alignment makes non-textual information more accessible during response generation. In summary, our findings uncover how Omni-LLMs can better express modality knowledge through language. Our code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Back-Translation Still Matters: Leveraging Monolingual Data for Low-Resource Machine Translation with LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18818)**  `arXiv:2610.18818`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Divyanshu Bathla, Parag Singla, Jitin Singla_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Pre-trained Large Language Model (LLMs) are effective on many tasks in zero-shot and few-shot settings. For machine translation of low-resource languages, the obvious options are few-shot prompting and fine-tuning on a small parallel set. We ask: what if moderate amounts of low-resource monolingual data are also available? We argue that, rather than continued pretraining, a more effective use of this data is the pre-LLM era technique of back-translation (BT). The current fine-tuned LLM translates monolingual sentences in each language, and the resulting pairs train it in the reverse direction. Updates on the parallel set are interleaved for stable learning. With 1K parallel pairs on Odia and Swahili, BT beats continued pretraining into the low-resource language by 7.7 to 16.4 XCOMET-XXL points in domain. With beam-decoded intermediate translations, it also beats a model with 10 time more parallel data. In-context examples retrieved from the parallel data further improve BT. We also analyze the source, quality and amount of monolingual text. Across five low-resource languages, with Hindi as a high-resource control, and two 3B backbones, BT improves translation into the low-resource language by 16 to 173% XCOMET-XXL over parallel-only fine-tuning. Blind human evaluation on Odia and Sanskrit agrees with the automatic metrics.
  </details>

- **[Where Do LLM Ensemble Gains Come From? Decomposing Candidate Value, Diversity, and Aggregation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18786)**  `arXiv:2610.18786`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Donghwan Kim_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  LLM ensemble gains are often measured against a single baseline, but the value attributed to additional candidates can change with the comparison used. We study an LLM aggregator under four matched conditions: Direct (no candidates), Single-slot (one candidate in a multi-slot interface), Duplicate (one candidate repeated), and Multi-candidate (separately generated candidates). Under either non-diverse control, overall candidate gain (CIV) splits algebraically into an additional-candidate contrast (DSV) and a candidate-context contrast (CCV); the split, but not CIV, depends on the chosen control. On MultiHopRAG model diversity (k=2), the repetition gap Rep=-8.33 pp [-13.25, -3.75] quantifies the difference between gains measured against Duplicate and Single-slot. On a matched FRAMES stronger-panel extension (n=200, k=3, aggregator output limit 4096), paired Delta Rep=+9.67 pp [+6.00, +13.50]; within panels, Rep changes sign (original -6.33; stronger +3.33). In FRAMES evidence aggregation, candidate-context contrasts remain strongly negative under both non-diverse controls. Our results show why ensemble evaluations should state the reference control before attributing gains to additional candidates.
  </details>

- **[From Relation-Specific Heads to Shared Interventions: Contextual Entrainment in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18674)**  `arXiv:2610.18674`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Jinghan Zheng, Jiajun Shi_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models rely on prompt context to perform in-context learning, follow formats, and adapt to local evidence. This ability, however, also raises a robustness concern: models may reuse irrelevant tokens from earlier context when answering a later query. Prior work identifies this behavior as contextual entrainment and finds attention heads whose ablation reduces it, arguing that these heads are largely task- or relation-specific. But are the mechanisms behind contextual entrainment truly isolated by relation, or do relation-conditioned searches recover reusable components shared across relations? Using factual-distractor relation-completion prompts across 19 lexical-semantic subtypes, we identify attention heads whose ablation reduces entrainment and test how the resulting head sets transfer recovery ability across exact relations, semantic families, and mixed relation distributions. Same-family transfer exceeds different-family transfer, family residuals weaken once globally shared heads are removed, and subtype-specific searches repeatedly rediscover many global heads. Clean-completion and context-use probes further suggest that this shared intervention can reduce harmful copying while preserving ordinary relation completion and simple in-context abilities. Our findings provide a more precise perspective on contextual entrainment and its mitigation: harmful context following is not best addressed by searching for isolated relation-specific circuits, but by using heterogeneous attack prompts to reveal reusable intervention targets whose effects are shaped by semantic relation structure.
  </details>

- **[Jev-ToM: Evaluating Theory of Mind in Typed Decision Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18610)**  `arXiv:2610.18610`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Kawai Chung, Chunkit Chan, Yuxuan Liu, Yauwai Yim, Xi Yang, Wenbin Hu, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Dialogue and collaborative assistants repeatedly judge what a partner knows, believes, or intends. Typed decision models offer a potential alternative to generative large language models for bounded Theory of Mind (ToM) selection. We present Jev-ToM, comparing five typed decision models and seven generative baselines on 11,117 English text questions from nine ToM benchmarks across six capability groups. TypeSafe Jev reaches 73.2% source-balanced accuracy including native controls and ranks first or second across all six capabilities, leading beliefs, goals/desires/intentions, and emotions. Other typed models show distinct strengths across tasks. Separate resource comparisons suggest that Jev could reduce the cost and waiting time of repeated ToM selection. Confidence-based selection remains benchmark-dependent, and supplied reasons can repair errors or overturn correct answers depending on their attachment. Candidate expansion reveals distinct selection and output-validity problems. Related-question cues account for most of Jev's downstream gains, with task-dependent effects from predicted states. The findings motivate testing Jev as a ToM selection component in assistants, with task-specific confidence calibration, candidate design, and output validation as integration priorities.
  </details>

- **[The Many Morals of AI: The cautionary bias of North American news narratives in global perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18573)**  `arXiv:2610.18573`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Andrew Piper, Edie Pearman_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The stories told about artificial intelligence (AI) play a central role in shaping public understanding, policy debates, and expectations about technological change. News media are especially influential in this process. Using a cross-regional corpus of 12,924 English-language news articles about AI published since 2022, we examine how storytelling about AI varies across media systems in four regions: North America, China, India, and the Middle East. Leveraging large language models, we extract the implicit narrative lessons conveyed by each article---commonly known as story morals---capturing value-laden interpretations that extend beyond thematic content or sentiment. We find that North American AI coverage is uniquely characterized by narratives of caution, while under-emphasizing narratives of innovation and collaboration that are more prevalent elsewhere. However, this pattern is largely explained by a broader regional negativity bias in North American news sentiment, rather than by heightened concern about AI itself. Our findings bring into view the culturally conditioned nature of AI news narratives.
  </details>

- **[Aligning Faithfulness for Theory-Scale Autoformalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18498)**  `arXiv:2610.18498`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Yuming Feng, Tadd Mao, Dhruva Arekar, Tianjun Zhong, Jiani Huang, Xujie Si, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Autoformalization (AF) requires more than compilation: formal statements must preserve the meaning of their informal sources, a property known as faithfulness. An emerging frontier is the automated evaluation of this property, yet most existing methods operate at the statement level and produce whole-item verdicts, failing to reveal how individual expressions correspond or which contextual interpretations support the judgment. This omission is consequential because AF is inherently theory-scale: target statements derive their meaning from surrounding mathematical material and unstated conventions. We formulate faithfulness evaluation as a context-aware align-then-label problem: identifying phrase-level correspondences between informal and formal statements and assigning a faithfulness label to each under explicitly specified contextual interpretations and assumptions. We also introduce FaithAlign, the first theory-scale faithfulness benchmark comprising 460 items and 4,982 annotated phrase-level links, alongside FaithAlign-Gap, a companion set of 146 items with informal context and assumptions withheld. Each FaithAlign item includes the target statement pair, relevant context, formal dependencies, and, where needed, assumptions specifying one given interpretation. Across 8 models, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest defect F1 at 47.8% and identifies all defects in only 4.5% of items with two or more defects. On FaithAlign-Gap, Astra identifies only 28.2% of undecidable items as such. These results show the difficulty of recovering context-dependent correspondences, establishing FaithAlign as a testbed for fine-grained, context-aware faithfulness evaluation.
  </details>

- **[Do Factuality Methods Make LLMs More Factual? Reproducibility and Fair Comparison](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18415)**  `arXiv:2610.18415`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Pratuat Amatya, Vinay Setty, V Venktesh, Avishek Anand_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to human preferences, after pre-training and supervised fine-tuning steps. However, standard RL alignment steps such as RLHF do not focus on factuality of LLMs, hence they may generate non-factual information, which could result in unintended consequences. In response, a number of factuality alignment approaches have been proposed in the literature which claim to improve factuality of LLMs on their own benchmarks. However, these methods have not been reproduced independently and are also not comparable since each uses a different base model, training data, evaluation set, judge, and metric. In this paper, we present the first independent reproduction of five factuality alignment methods, which span on-policy RL (PPO, GRPO, and Dr.~GRPO) and offline preference optimization (DPO and KTO), and compare them on a common benchmark with common evaluation metrics. We found that none of these methods reproduces in full, and on the common benchmark none of the methods significantly outperforms the base model. On closer inspection, the rewards optimize for format, length, or brevity rather than factuality and relevance, whereas the choice between on-policy and offline training matters little. Furthermore, the evaluation metrics and benchmarks are also part of the problem since they do not measure relevance of text to the prompt. Since there is no ground truth associated with the prompts, the reliance on LLM judges and retrieval for verification also makes the evaluation fragile. We release our code, data, and checkpoints.
  </details>

- **[Lightweight but Linguistically Fair? Quantisation Robustness across Bavarian, German, and English](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18343)**  `arXiv:2610.18343`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Jophin John, Michael Hoffmann, Piroska Lendvai, Florent Dufour_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Post-training quantisation reduces the memory cost of large language models, but it remains unclear whether compression preserves language skills of regional varieties as reliably as their standard-language counterparts. We study this question for Bavarian, Standard German, and English using BAVGROUND, a multiple-choice benchmark, where 206 source questions are aligned across all three languages. Across 14 open-weight 7B--10B instruction models, we compare BF16 with 8-bit GPTQ and two 4-bit settings, GPTQ and AWQ. Eight-bit GPTQ remains close to BF16 and largely preserves the relative behaviour of the three languages, while 4-bit quantisation was found to be much less stable. The two 4-bit methods reduce average accuracy by about 1.4--1.5 percentage points and change 11.9--16.0% of BF16 decisions, with changes concentrated on examples where the BF16 model is already uncertain. This instability does not translate into a consistent Bavarian disadvantage. Although Bavarian, a low-resource dialect, has lower baseline accuracy than German and English, the language most affected at 4 bits varies across models and quantisation methods. Calibration further shapes these cross-language effects: the relative Bavarian--German effect changes with calibration language, while changing the calibration source has little average effect on GPTQ-4 but can affect AWQ-4 much more strongly. Free-form evaluation on five models further shows that 4-bit compression can degrade generated responses even in settings where multiple-choice accuracy changes only modestly, while 8-bit GPTQ remains comparatively stable. Overall, our results show that quantisation robustness for regional language varieties depends on the model, quantisation method, calibration data, and evaluation setting, and cannot be measured by aggregate multilingual accuracy alone.
  </details>

- **[TextualRL: Textual Reinforcement Learning for Context Management](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18216)**  `arXiv:2610.18216`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Tianyu Huai, Jie Zhou, Bo Mao, Qin Chen, Liang He, Xipeng Qiu_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  LLM agents can adapt to task feedback by revising the textual context that guides their behavior, without changing their model parameters. However, turning execution rewards into reusable context updates is challenging: individual trajectories offer limited comparative evidence about what to change, while task-specific fixes may overgeneralize when incorporated into a shared context. We introduce TextualRL, a gradient-free reinforcement learning framework that treats a group of rollouts from the same task under the same context, rather than an isolated trajectory, as the unit of policy critique. Groupwise Policy Critique contrasts successful and failed rollouts within a task; when outcomes are uniform, it draws on cross-task evidence to identify behaviors worth preserving or formulate repair hypotheses. Cross-Group Policy Update reviews the resulting proposals against evidence pooled across groups, including observations that yield no proposed edit, to refine their content and applicability. Reviewed proposals form a bounded textual patch, with adoption of the candidate context determined by held-out validation rewards. Together, these components establish a reward-driven policy optimization loop in which multiple attempts jointly inform reusable context updates. We evaluate TextualRL with five target agents on six benchmarks. Averaged over the six benchmarks, TextualRL improves test accuracy over the base model by 24.4 and 15.3 percentage points for GPT-5.5 and Qwen3.8-27B, respectively.
  </details>

- **[Claim Framing as a Driver of LLM Sycophancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18159)**  `arXiv:2610.18159`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Jean Seo, Pepa Atanasova, Isabelle Augenstein_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Sycophancy in Large Language Models, the tendency to align responses with user preferences over ground truth, has largely been studied using questions without a clear ground truth and with a single, plainly stated user opinion. We present a systematic study of which framings of a user's claim trigger sycophancy in factual question answering, where every answer is objectively verifiable without extra context. Evaluating 14 models on 42K questions, we express correct and incorrect user opinions through various claim framings over 8 dimensions and 21 types, and measure a broad set of opinion-driven behaviors. We find that all models are susceptible to user opinions regardless of size. Models are most influenced by how confidently an opinion is stated, whom it is attributed to, and whether it is presented as shared between the user and the model. In contrast to prior work, framings based on the user's expertise, authority over the model, or social pressure matter little in our factual setting. Larger models resist incorrect opinions better but are no better at recovering from their own errors. Our results call for sycophancy evaluations that probe how an opinion is framed, not merely whether one is present, and that measure multiple behaviors beyond a single flip rate.
  </details>

- **[Virtual Head Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17959)**  `arXiv:2610.17959`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Xibo Ding, Guoxia Wang, Jinle Zeng, Jiabin Yang, Sirui Tao, Chao Yang, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The design of attention mechanisms in long-context large language models faces an ``impossible triangle'' among KV cache size, training and prefill FLOPs, and model quality. GQA achieves strong quality but incurs high KV cache overhead; alternative approaches such as MLA and MFA can compress the cache, but MLA suffers from quality loss while MFA substantially increases training and prefill compute. We propose Virtual Head Attention (VHA), which simultaneously improves all three vertices through two lightweight linear operations: Q Premix applies a near-identity transformation to queries within each KV group to recover virtual head diversity from halved physical query heads, and Linear Postmix fuses inter-head features via a low-rank $I + AB^\top$ residual structure. Since VHA introduces no nonlinear operations, Premix can be folded into the query projection and Postmix into the output projection at inference time, reducing the model to a standard GQA-2 architecture that directly reuses all existing GQA inference optimizations. With only two KV heads, the group size in large models readily reaches 64, fully exploiting Tensor Core parallelism during decoding. Across four scales with 4K-context 50B-token pretraining, VHA consistently surpasses the standard GQA baseline at every scale ($+$0.05\% to $+$0.81\%), while reducing KV cache by $4\times$ vs.\ GQA-8 at dense scales and $2\times$ vs.\ GQA-4 at the MoE scale, and lowering training and prefill FLOPs by 7.9\% (1.7B, $S{=}4096$). On an industrial 30B-A3B MoE model trained on 500B tokens at 8K context, VHA outperforms both MLA and GQA-4 by $+$0.70\,/\,$+$2.60\,\% on a 12-benchmark base-model evaluation suite; in a separate matched 10B-A1B MoE comparison after long-context mid-training, VHA attains an average RULER score of 84.4 over 8K--128K versus 73.0 for GQA, while using two rather than four KV heads in the full-attention layers.
  </details>

- **[Cross-Lingual Transfer of Evil Vectors Is Directionally Asymmetric](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17880)**  `arXiv:2610.17880`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Juann Kim, Minku Kang_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Persona vectors are linear directions in the residual-stream activations of LLMs that encode behavioral traits and enable fine-grained control over model behavior. Among them, the evil persona vector is particularly relevant to understanding harmful behavior, jailbreak vulnerabilities, and the unlearning of harmful knowledge. Yet whether this vector reflects a genuinely cross-lingual concept, rather than an artifact of its extraction language, remains untested. We conduct a systematic evil-vector transfer study across two high-resource languages (English, Spanish) and two low-resource languages (Swahili, Telugu) on four open-source instruction-tuned LLMs, and find that transfer is directionally asymmetric. Evil vectors are harder to obtain reliably from low-resource languages, and the resulting vectors are largely ineffective at steering, even within their own language. In contrast, vectors extracted from high-resource languages transfer effectively to low-resource inputs while largely preserving general knowledge, as measured by MMLU. Geometric analysis further supports this pattern: evil vectors from the two high-resource languages are closely aligned, whereas low-resource vectors align only weakly with this shared direction. These results suggest that a shared cross-lingual evil direction exists and, once reliably extracted from a high-resource language, can be reused to steer behavior in low-resource languages without additional per-language data collection.
  </details>

- **[Many Steps into One: Reasoning Contraction and the Limits of Safe Memory Reuse for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17544)**  `arXiv:2610.17544`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Jianghong Zhou, Hao Rong, Chen Lin, Daoan Zhang_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Thought templates, skill libraries, agent memories and caches turn many reasoning steps into one. We call this reasoning contraction. A contracted memory saves reasoning steps and errors until its facts change, then quietly answers wrong. Most systems trust memories by counting successes and failures. We prove that such counters are badly tuned change detectors: a symmetric counter notices a partial change only after a power of its false-alarm horizon, and an unclipped one may never notice it. On five LLMs answering multi-hop questions over edited facts, ExpeL- and ACE-style counters serve 7.0-13.5x more stale answers than certified memories given the same information, and on code tasks with an exact verifier 35-73x more. Safety also has a price. When facts change and each memory is judged only by its own verified outcomes, one number, the certification load, sets how much reasoning any safe memory can skip, and under Zipf demand it yields a scaling law. Our recipe weighs each memory's failures by its own likelihood ratio, certifies its utility against live reasoning, and restarts the certificate when facts change, with the likelihood-ratio detector as the safety net for unannounced changes; for large edits it also invalidates the memory.
  </details>

- **[StartLux-Decision: AutoThink Decision Models with Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17309)**  `arXiv:2610.17309`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Xialie Zhuang, Zunhai Su, Jia Pan, Ngai Wong, Guanhua Chen, Chuan-Wei Kuo_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We introduce StartLux-Decision, decision models from 0.8B to 27B parameters that combine efficient single-pass prediction with adaptive, confidence-guided reasoning. The Instant models use bidirectional attention in full-attention layers to improve decision accuracy while keeping single-pass inference. The AutoThink models invoke explicit reasoning for uncertain decisions and answer confident cases directly. We also introduce DecisionPivot, a programmatically verifiable benchmark of computational decisions built from contrast pairs that differ in a single answer-changing detail. On DecisionPivot, AutoThink outperforms its Instant counterparts by 11.5-18.4 points in pair accuracy and leads among evaluated systems. The models run on vLLM,this http URLand MLX, with quantized variants for lower memory use.

- **[Query Your Way Out: Benchmarking Multi-Turn Knowledge Reasoning through Generalized Puzzle Solving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16133)**  `arXiv:2610.16133`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Xin Cheng, Junming Yang, Ning Xu_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>

  </details>

- **[Review Rarely Beats the Stronger Model: Separating Verification from Capability Transfer in LLM Pipelines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15897)**  `arXiv:2610.15897`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`

  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>

Measured against the stronger model alone, across 48 pairs of 12 open-weight models (3B to 72B) in math, knowledge, code and reasoning, review beats it in only 9 of 96 review directions, and does worse the larger the capability gap. The reason is that the reviewer mostly follows the generator, discarding its own correct answers. Review costs 2.6 to 2.8 times as much as the stronger model alone, while a selector using the same two calls is 2.7 to 4.2 points more accurate than review and cheaper. Studies of verification should report the stronger model alone, not only the gain over the generator. Code and per-question results:this https URL
  </details>

- **[North or South? Diagnosing LLMs' Understanding of North Korean Language, Society, and Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15282)**  `arXiv:2610.15282`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Kiwoong Park, Seyoung Song, Donghyun Woo, Alice Oh_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large Language Models (LLMs) have made substantial progress in multilingual question answering, yet their ability to understand low-resource sociolinguistic contexts remains under-explored. We study North Korea as a unique testbed where decades of division have produced distinct differences from South Korea in vocabulary, orthography, norms, and ideological discourse. We introduce LENS (Language and sociocultural Evaluation for North Korean Society), a human-validated benchmark of 1,765 questions evaluating LLMs across three dimensions: linguistic robustness, sociocultural perspective alignment, and domain-specific knowledge.   </details>

- **[UDHRBench: Benchmarking Human Rights in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15179)**  `arXiv:2610.15179`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Alak Raad, Noreldin Morssy, Zeerak Suhail, Serin Atiani, Mustafa Jarrar_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models are increasingly deployed in contexts requiring adherence to ethical and legal norms, yet their alignment with internationally recognized human rights standards remains underexplored. We introduce UDHRBench, a large-scale benchmark for operationalising the evaluation of large language model compliance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Our analysis reveals systematic and non-trivial misalignments, showing that violations typically arise through seemingly rational reasoning: appeals to efficiency, risk management, or scientific neutrality, rather than explicit rejection of rights. We further propose an LLM-as-a-Judge framework for automated evaluation using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, achieving 89.8\% weighted F1-score in detecting human-rights misalignment, alongside a novel Alignment Leniency Score that quantifies how judge models resolve ambiguous cases. The dataset, annotations, and code will be released as open-source resources (this https URL).
  </details>

- **[Select or Rewrite: Oracle-Guided Fine-Tuning for Generative ASR Post-Editing from N-Best Hypotheses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15056)**  `arXiv:2610.15056`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`

  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>

  </details>

- **[Toward System One Clinical Intelligence: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning and Counterfactual Explainability of Decision Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15029)**  `arXiv:2610.15029`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _S. M. Mahbub Uddin Ahmed_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>

Using 4-bit quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) with differential learning rates and a stratified split of 960 training and 240 test cases, the model achieves 95.42% diagnostic accuracy and a macro F1 score of 0.9551. This improves upon the reported zero-shot baselines of 61.67% for a remote API and 65.00% for a local unadapted initialization, and outperforms the ClinicalBERT baseline (90.90%). By evaluating candidate logits in a single forward pass without autoregressive decoding, inference takes under 80 milliseconds per record on a single GPU, yielding a reported 31-fold speedup over generative LLM baselines. To examine symptom-level evidence, we introduce a Leave-One-Symptom-Out (LOSO) counterfactual perturbation framework. Removing disease-defining symptom clauses in a psoriasis example reduces predicted-class confidence from 100.00% to 0.12% and shifts the prediction to impetigo with 99.59% confidence, while removing secondary systemic symptoms produces less than 0.01% change in confidence.   </details>

- **[UltraBERT: Beyond the Limit of BERT Pre-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15028)**  `arXiv:2610.15028`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Jungwoo Park, Taewhoo Lee, Jaewoo Kang_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent bidirectional encoders have been modernized with innovations from causal large language models (LLMs). However, the pretraining recipe itself remains inherited from small-scale conventions, leaving encoders underoptimized, with no single model performing competitively across both classification and retrieval tasks. In this work, we investigate how far encoder performance can be pushed by revisiting core design choices in training, revealing three key findings: (1) Encoders saturate on downstream tasks beyond a few trillion tokens, indicating that additional compute past this point does not help. (2) Across model sizes, lower masking ratios benefit classification while higher ones benefit retrieval, contradicting prior work suggesting larger ratios for larger models. (3) Distillation with pruning improves classification at low masking ratios but degrades retrieval at high ones. Guided by these findings, we present UltraBERT, a single encoder that assigns separate LM heads to low and high masking ratios within a batch and restricts the distillation objective to the low ratio. To our knowledge, UltraBERT is the first encoder to achieve state of the art on both classification and retrieval tasks, reaching 91.0 on GLUE and 47.7 on BEIR. Together, these results show how far encoder performance can be pushed and provide a principled basis for compute allocation, masking ratio design, and knowledge transfer in bidirectional models.
  </details>

- **[Vela: User Behavior as Supervision Sparks LLM Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14709)**  `arXiv:2610.14709`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Yang Xiao, Yusong Sun, Haoyi Wu, Wenyang Hui, Weiqiang Hang, Luqing Wang, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models are increasingly deployed in applications that act on users' long-term behavior histories, from personal assistants to recommendation and advertising systems. These applications demand the user dimension of LLM intelligence: inferring a person's preferences, intent, and likely future actions from weeks to years of behavior data. Yet current models are trained on static text or synthetic data, neither of which captures how user behavior evolves over time. Real-world behavior records, already available at scale on content platforms and in personal-assistant agents, offer a natural supervisory signal. We propose user behavior as supervision and introduce Vela, a framework that converts real user behavior data into trainable tasks and trajectories. From the anonymized behavior records of 100,000 users, Vela generates 100,000 tasks across 91 real-world task templates; difficulty-based filtering and trajectory acceptance criteria retain approximately 75,000 tasks with selected training trajectories. Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on these trajectories improves performance over the base model by up to 11.5 points on user-related tasks and by an average of 4 points on general benchmarks. Training on more user behavior data further improves user-related performance, and reinforcement learning after fine-tuning outperforms reinforcement learning from the base model by up to 7.7 points. These gains suggest that real-world user behavior is a scalable source of supervision for both user-centered capabilities and the broader intelligence of LLMs.
  </details>

- **[Lingdan-V2: Large language models for clinically grounded reasoning in traditional Chinese medicine](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14705)**  `arXiv:2610.14705`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Rui Hua, Yu Wei, Ziri Jin, Zhuo Sun, Kai Chang, Jianan Xia, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models have advanced medical reasoning, but clinically grounded reasoning in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) remains challenging because prescription decisions require integrating domain knowledge, syndrome differentiation, treatment principles, herbal prescription composition, and dosage determination. We develop a TCM language model family comprising models with 4 billion, 8 billion, and 14 billion parameters. The artificial intelligence contribution is a staged clinical alignment framework integrating large scale continued pretraining on TCM and clinical records, complementary reasoning supervision, and prescription-centered reinforcement learning (RL). We further formulate herbal prescription generation as a structured RL problem with prescription-level feedback, enabling direct optimization of clinical decision outputs beyond knowledge reproduction and generic instruction following. The engineering application is TCM clinical decision support, particularly herbal prescription recommendation. We evaluate the models on a public benchmark containing 25,620 expert-verified items across 13 TCM knowledge and clinical reasoning tasks and on a private retrospective dataset of 4,348 spleen and stomach disease prescription cases. The 14 billion parameter reinforcement aligned model achieves a prescription generation F1 of 37.0 on the public benchmark, compared with 32.3 for DeepSeek-R1 with 671 billion total parameters, and a herb-level F1 of 52.8 on the clinical dataset with improved dosage agreement. Reinforcement post-training consistently improves prescription recommendation across all scales, while physician-source analysis shows that expert heterogeneity affects reward stability. These findings demonstrate a scalable pathway from domain grounding and reasoning supervision to clinically oriented prescription decision support.
  </details>

- **[Scale, Drivers, and Limits of Representational Alignment Across Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14476)**  `arXiv:2610.14476`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Jialin Wu, Meenakshi Khosla_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Comparing large language models can reveal shared representational structure and systematic differences between them. However, aggregate similarity measures can obscure how agreement varies across geometric scales and which linguistic properties support it. We introduce two complementary methods to resolve where models agree and what supports that agreement. Standard representational similarity analysis (RSA) summarizes similarity across all stimulus pairs, potentially obscuring differences in alignment between nearby and distant inputs. Neighborhood-Weighted RSA (NW-RSA) addresses this limitation by weighting stimulus pairs according to their proximity in representational space, placing alignment from local neighborhoods to global geometry on a common scale. Counterfactual RSA (CF-RSA) tests which linguistic properties support alignment by comparing intact representations in one model with representations under controlled linguistic perturbations in another. Across diverse language models, we find strong agreement in coarse representational geometry but substantial divergence in local neighborhoods. Alignment is observed both across broadly sampled natural text and within linguistic equivalence classes that preserve particular aspects of meaning or structure. Counterfactual analyses reveal selective sensitivity: changes to logical scope reduce alignment substantially more than the tested changes to hierarchical syntax, event roles, or discourse structure. Alignment also decreases when sentence structure or lexical meaning is disrupted in word lists and jabberwocky sentences, suggesting that the regularities of natural language support stronger convergence. These findings refine claims of representational universality by showing that strong overall similarity need not imply agreement in how models represent finer linguistic distinctions.
  </details>

- **[Is the Future Predictable? Modeling Future Predictability for Reliable Temporal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14073)**  `arXiv:2610.14073`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Yongyi Huang, Huaping Zhang, Wenyao Cui, Qiuchi Li, Lei Li, Baohua Zhang_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) remain unreliable when reasoning about the future. Existing models often overlook the difference among future states, committing to specific answers even when the queried facts are inherently volatile. To capture this challenge, we introduce ChronoRegime, a future-oriented temporal reasoning task that requires models to determine whether historical temporal evidence justifies commitment to a future answer. Furthermore, we propose Confidence-Aware Temporal Reasoning (CTR), a framework that estimates future predictability from temporal dynamics and regulates answer commitment accordingly. Rather than performing unconditional forecasting, CTR commits only when the reconstructed evidence supports the target future state. Across multiple LLMs, CTR improves strict overall accuracy by 6.7 percentage points and reduces hallucination rates by 18.4 percentage points on average over the plain QA baseline. These results demonstrate that explicit predictability assessment is an effective mechanism for safer and more reliable temporal reasoning under future uncertainty.
  </details>

- **[Loose Lips: Understanding Privacy Leakage in Agentic Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14071)**  `arXiv:2610.14071`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Soumya Sharma, Ayana Hussain, Heber Hwang Arcolezi, Ulrich Aïvodji, Spandana Gella, Adriana Romero-Soriano, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  As LLM agents are increasingly deployed in high-stakes enterprise settings, understanding how they handle sensitive information in agentic dialogue has become critical. Privacy leakage in such settings requires reasoning about whether information flows respect the contextual norms under which they originated. We extend CIMemories to CIMEMORIES DIALOGUE, a benchmark of 4,410 two-agent dialogue instances grounded in Contextual Integrity theory. Using this benchmark, we systematically evaluate 7 open-weight models from the Qwen3 and Llama 3.1 families across conversation lengths of 1 and 6 turns under three prompting conditions. We find that task capability and privacy leakage are fundamentally coupled: more capable models are systematically leakier, with no model in our evaluation able to decouple the two. Thinking models consistently leak more than their non-thinking counterparts, a pattern we attribute to the extended reasoning surface created by chain-of-thought. Leakage compounds with conversation length, rising up to 3x from 1 to 6 turns. Our results suggest that the coupling between task capability and privacy leakage is not an artifact of misconfiguration but a structural feature of current agentic systems.
  </details>

- **[Constitutional Gating and Deterministic Recovery for Multi-Agent LLM Negotiation: Ablations Against a Stateful Adversarial Gatekeeper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11542)**  `arXiv:2610.11542`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Masaaki Nakatsu, Reno Wang_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multi-agent LLM systems negotiating with a stateful counterpart waste model calls in three ways: polite loops that never meet the counterpart's hidden acceptance condition, malformed outputs that trigger retries, and compliance deadlocks in which the counterpart demands something the agent must refuse. We study a three-part control stack - a 5-Pillar runtime constitution, a 4-tier swarm (Director, three-agent majority vote, Monitor, schema hard gate) and Cognitive Annealing (deterministic deadlock detection, atomic purge of the agent-side context, a canonical recovery message) - against a released adversarial Gatekeeper whose acceptance rules are fixed regular expressions and whose LLM only renders reply text. The testbed has a known solution: it measures whether the stack executes a constitution-aligned strategy against swarm drift and recovers from deadlock, not whether it discovers anything. In five runs per configuration (30 runs; Gemini 2.5 Pro agents, Claude Haiku 4.5 Gatekeeper) we find: (i) the constitution and Director make an acceptable framing possible but not reliable - 0/5 baseline unlocks versus 1/5 and 2/5 with the constitution; when the swarm unlocks it does so in one turn with 7-8 calls and about 15k tokens (67-73% below baseline); when it does not, it costs 17-38% more; (ii) the Monitor and hard gate do not reduce unlocks and leave an audit trail; (iii) under a honeytrap-to-compliance deadlock, LLM-only steering escapes 0 of 5 times while atomic purge plus a canonical strike escapes 5 of 5 (Fisher $p = 0.008$) at the same call budget, with zero calls for the strike. LLM-written strikes failed the deterministic pre-flight 5 of 5 times although an LLM Monitor had approved four. Pre-registered hypotheses on average call and token reduction were not supported. Cost is bounded in every arm by deterministic stop rules; the stack adds recovery at no extra model cost.
  </details>

- **[REMORY: Learning Residual Memory for Context Compaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11287)**  `arXiv:2610.11287`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Hanchen Xia, Baoyou Chen, Yutang Ge, Naihao Deng, Senqiao Yang, Zilong Dong, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>

The tokens are conditioned on the summary and appended after it, forming an analogue of a residual connection along the sequence dimension. On SummHay, REMORY improves source attribution at nearly unchanged insight coverage and approaches the full-context joint score using only 5.2% of the input positions. Across long-horizon agent benchmarks, Qwen3.8-27B and GLM-5.3-Flash show consistent gains with residual memory. Both models also exhibit substantially fewer repeated tool outputs and tool errors on BrowseComp and Terminal-Bench 2.1.
  </details>

- **[Grammar Concept Annotation at Scale: Deployed Fine-Tuned Small Language Models Outperform Prompted Frontier Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10827)**  `arXiv:2610.10827`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Marjan Celikik, Ana Peleteiro Ramallo, Javier Morales_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Corrective feedback is among the best-evidenced drivers of second-language acquisition, yet corrections delivered during lessons rarely accumulate into an actionable view of grammar mastery. We close this gap by fine-tuning Qwen3.5 small language models (SLMs) on filtered and rebalanced teacher-generated supervision, then deploying an efficient 0.8B model in an end-to-end grammar mastery tracker for all English learners on our platform. On two human-curated benchmarks, both the deployed 0.8B model and a 4B reference comparator outperform prompted GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.6 Sol in precision and recall under nested matching criteria of increasing strictness: concept, evidence span, and correctness. A feature-level online experiment shows significant gains in learner engagement ($+15.8\%$) and key business metrics, including scheduled hours ($+2.1\%$) and GMV from new lessons ($+13.2\%$).
  </details>

- **[Ready2Blend: From Natural-Language Instructions to Composable Alignment Prompts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39365)**  `arXiv:2609.39365`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Jeesu Jung, Hwan Chang, Juseon Do, Jeonghwan Choi, Jinho Choo, Sungwoo Nam, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>

  </details>

- **[Structure vs. Chain-of-Thought: Evaluating LLM Criteria Extraction for Depression Severity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39049)**  `arXiv:2609.39049`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Xinkai Chen_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>

The latter is easier to audit because a clinician can check each marked criterion. We compare these approaches on two Reddit corpora using three LLMs (from 9B to frontier scale) and two questionnaires (PHQ-9, BDI-II), and measure agreement with quadratic weighted kappa. For the two frontier models, criteria extraction scores above chain-of-thought on one corpus only when its decision thresholds are fitted on labeled data. Neither model's gain is significant, with or without recalibrating chain-of-thought on the same labels. With thresholds fixed a priori from PHQ-9's criteria, extraction shows no gain on either corpus, even where models mark over two criteria per post. The 9B model behaves differently on a corpus from depression communities. It labels most posts as severe, whether prompted directly or with chain-of-thought, while the a priori rule, which uses no labels, beats both. After chain-of-thought is recalibrated on the same labels, no significant gap remains, consistent with a calibration effect. Yet higher ordinal agreement does not ensure better detection of severe cases. PHQ-9 criteria extraction misses most severe posts, and moving from direct prompting to chain-of-thought and then to extraction increases misses in nearly all comparisons. On one corpus, a relabeled stress dataset, a model using that dataset's own features, some computed from the post text, is not significantly different from frontier criteria extraction under the a priori rule.
  </details>

- **[LLM Alignment--Utility Asymmetry under Semantic-Preserving Transformations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32717)**  `arXiv:2609.32717`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Mohan Li, Chengyu Yu, Francesco Sovrano, Marc Langheinrich, Martin Gjoreski_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large Language Model (LLM) alignment is intended to ensure that models remain helpful and safe, but its stability under input distributional shift is not yet fully understood. Prior work shows that aligned models can fail under jailbreak prompts, alternative encodings, and cross-lingual transfer, yet these failures are usually studied as attacks rather than controlled probes of alignment generalization. Moreover, existing evidence is largely grounded in natural language variation already represented during pretraining, leaving unresolved whether alignment generalizes with semantic content or remains tied to superficial surface patterns. In this paper, we study this question using synthetic semantic-preserving transformations that are rule-based and invertible, preserving task-relevant meaning while shifting inputs beyond standard linguistic variation. Across four open-weight and four commercial models, under both fine-tuning and in-context learning, we use these transformations as a probe of alignment generalization and identify an empirical pattern we term Alignment--utility asymmetry: once models can operate effectively on transformed inputs, task utility is often substantially retained while alignment failure increases more sharply. For example, adapted GPT-4.1 mini shows only limited utility degradation under transformation while its harmful rate rises from 13.3 to 74.3; Gemini 3 Flash similarly retains near-original utility while its harmful rate increases from 2.3 to 43.0. Taken together, these results suggest that semantic-preserving distribution shifts can expose a recurring gap in how utility and alignment generalize in current LLMs.
  </details>

- **[R-DEIM Net: An Efficient Rationale-Augmented Dual-Expert Interaction Model for Paraphrase Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30100)**  `arXiv:2609.30100`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Pushp Garg, Vaibhav Prajapati, Himangshu Sarma_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>

The architecture combines two specialized components: an Interaction Expert that captures token-level similarity patterns through multi-scale 2D convolutions and attention head allowing variable input length, and a Reasoning Expert that uses a Flan-T5-small decoder to generate rationales as auxiliary supervision. Rather than re-encoding generated text, we extract and pool decoder hidden states as complementary features for classification. On the Quora Question Pairs dataset, R-DEIM Net achieves 90.07% accuracy and 90.16% F1-score via 10-fold cross-validation. This represents competitive performance with strong transformer-based baselines (e.g., MFAE BERT: 90.54% accuracy) and recent large language model based approaches (LLaMA-70B) while using a substantially smaller parameter budget. The model generates rationales alongside predictions, providing potential for auxiliary human-readable descriptions.
  </details>

- **[Beyond Unsafe Detection: Counterfactually Anchored Evidence Attribution for Multi-Turn LLM Safety Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27773)**  `arXiv:2609.27773`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Srinivasan Subramanian, Kazi Aminul Islam, Md. Abdullah Al Hafiz Khan_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  As Large Language Models (LLMs) move from conversational assistants to advanced agentic systems, guardrail failures can convert adversarial intents into harmful executions. However, most evaluation frameworks focus only on whether a user request is unsafe. This is insufficient for multi-turn failures, where adversarial intent may be distributed across turns and emerge only from accumulated context. This motivates us to go beyond detection to localize the evidence that pushes the conversation toward unsafe trajectories. We introduce MTAG-Bench, a multi-turn guardrail attribution dataset with behavioral validation and counterfactual supervision containing 4,167 conversations. We also introduce MTAG-Probe, a hierarchical attribution model for turn- and span-level evidence localization with conversation-level safety detection. MTAG-Probe improves turn-level F1 by 28.1 and 24.1 points (79.0% and 61.0% relative) over self-attribution by the model that produced the unsafe response and the LLM safety-judge attribution, respectively. Removing MTAG-Probe's top-ranked evidence within budgets of 15% and 20% of user words per conversation changes 50.6% and 60.8% of Llama Guard decisions on Geometry from unsafe to safe, respectively. In full-trajectory replay, MTAG-Probe converts 84.3% of eligible unsafe final responses to safe. These results show that MTAG-Probe can provide evidence-level explanations as a practical complement to safety detection.
  </details>

- **[When Context Misleads: In-context Learning with Jurisdiction in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27603)**  `arXiv:2609.27603`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Pei-lin Li, Qingle Liu, Junyang Feng, Siyu Li, Sunqi Fan, Xin-Sheng Chen, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In-Context Learning (ICL) has become a cornerstone of modern LLM deployment. However, existing ICL post-training methods have a critical blind spot: they excel at extracting patterns from demonstrations while often neglecting context authority, the ability to determine whether contextual information should govern the final answer. To benchmark this capability, we introduce FakeContextBench, which contains pseudoscientific claims across seven domains. Our evaluation of commercial and open-source models shows that large-scale pre-training alone is insufficient for reliable context-authority discrimination. Moreover, prevalent ICL fine-tuning methods can increase susceptibility to misleading context, reducing reality accuracy by up to 14.95 percentage points relative to the base model. To address this trade-off, we propose Jurisdiction In-Context Learning (J-ICL), a post-training framework that incorporates context validation into the training objective. Across four model backbones, J-ICL improves ICLEval by an average of 5.84 percentage points and reality accuracy by 9.20 points over the corresponding base models. It also raises the Reality Rate by an average of 18.09 points relative to MetaICL and Symbol Tuning. These results demonstrate that ICL capability and resistance to deceptive context can be improved together. The benchmark is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[SPINE: Measuring LLM Sycophancy under Sustained Multi-Turn Pressure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.09090)**  `arXiv:2609.09090`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Leyuan Tang, Kangda Wei, Tianyu Jiang, Ruihong Huang_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) may abandon correct positions when users push back, exhibiting a failure mode known as sycophancy. Existing evaluations typically use short, prespecified conversations and may therefore miss failures that emerge under sustained, adaptive disagreement. We introduce SPINE, a benchmark in which an LLM proxy plays a persistent but mistaken user and adaptively challenges a target model for up to 25 turns. We evaluate four commercial models (Claude Sonnet 5, GPT-5.6 Terra, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and DeepSeek V4 Pro) and three Olmo3-7b models on 100 false presuppositions and 100 unethical queries. We define collapse as a target model abandoning the correct position and yielding to user pressure. Our experimental results show that collapse rates increase with conversation length across post-trained models, with the overall rate rising from 0%-57% within 5 turns to 20%-97% within 25 turns depending on model and scenario. These results show that evaluations limited to a few conversational turns underestimate sycophancy and resistance under sustained pressure remains unreliable across current models. By analyzing models with accessible reasoning traces, we surprisingly found that the correct position often remains represented in the trace in 50%-89% of analyzed collapse turns, suggesting that the model chooses to please a user and sycophancy is not due to ignorance or the correct knowledge being overridden. Ablations show that the SPINE protocol substantially increases the sycophantic collapse rate compared to pre-generated scripts. Among all tactics, emotional appeals are most associated with inducing LLM sycophantic behavior, with position weakening in 44.3% of turns using this tactic. Code, data, and transcripts will be released upon publication.
  </details>

- **[A, B, C, or Stable? Accuracy and Order Sensitivity Diverge in LLM Multiple-Choice Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11947)**  `arXiv:2608.11947`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Karl Hanna, Chen Feng_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multiple-choice question (MCQ) benchmarks are widely used to evaluate large language models, yet a single reported accuracy number is not enough to distinguish a model's latent ability from order sensitivity. Debiasing methods tend to be judged on one axis, which implicitly assumes that fixing order sensitivity and improving accuracy go together. We test this assumption with two proprietary models and two open-weight models on MMLU and ARC-Challenge, across four families of strategies. We measure order sensitivity with flip rate, capturing per-question instability, and recall standard deviation (RStd), capturing aggregate positional imbalance. We find accuracy and order sensitivity do not move together consistently: two-stage prompting reduces both flip rate and RStd for GPT on MMLU without a significant change in accuracy. The two sensitivity metrics also diverge from each other. Adding reasoning to direct answering leaves Llama's MMLU flip rate statistically indistinguishable while RStd falls sharply. A $2\times2$ ablation across generation-then-matching, crossing option visibility with matcher type, shows that withholding options mainly harms semantic matching, which achieves zero flip rate by construction, yet loses significantly in accuracy; the effect is smaller when using an LLM matcher. We recommend reporting flip rate and RStd along with accuracy when evaluating MCQ strategies.
  </details>

- **[Lost in Context Compaction: When LLM Systems Drop Side Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11242)**  `arXiv:2608.11242`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Zhiqi Wang, Yichi Zhang, Dongwon Lee, Nathalie Baracaldo, Yuchen Yang_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  When the context window is under pressure, LLM systems compact prior context to continue ongoing tasks. We study Side Constraints (SCs), user-issued instructions such as "do not delete any emails until I confirm," that constrain an LLM's behavior across subsequent turns but can be silently dropped during compaction. In an inbox experiment, an agent deleted emails without approval in 30/100 sessions after compaction, compared with none before compaction. To systematically evaluate SC preservation, we introduce CONPACT, an evaluation suite measuring semantic retention and downstream compliance across three scenarios: multi-turn chat, multi-turn tool use, and long-horizon research.The evaluated compactors retain only 17% of injected SCs on average. Loss occurs across compactors and settings, with retention varying by compactor, context length, SC framing, and injection location. We propose an SC extractor that maintains constraints separately from the task summary and appends them to the compacted context, achieving over 90% retention across all three scenarios without modifying the compactor or LLM. Code and data are available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Search-G1: Co-Evolving Representation-Based Rewards for Selective Grounded Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07531)**  `arXiv:2608.07531`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Ruoxi Cheng, Haoxuan Ma, Hongyi Zhang, Junming Zhang, Ranjie Duan, Qiaolin Xia, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Search-augmented language agents should retrieve external information only when necessary and ground their answers in retrieved evidence. Yet terminal correctness assigns equal credit to direct answers from parametric knowledge, evidence-grounded answers, and answers recalled after redundant search. Process supervision and LLM judges provide richer feedback but can require high-cost annotation or inference; low-cost, non-contrastive policy confidence signals do not directly identify whether retrieved evidence changes an answer. We propose Search-G1, a reward framework that couples retrieval necessity with evidence reliance through two intervention-calibrated hidden-state readouts for selective grounded search. A prompt readout predicts closed-book sufficiency, whose complement proxies policy-relative retrieval necessity; an answer-commit readout predicts evidence reliance as sensitivity to evidence deletion conditional on the realized reasoning prefix. A correctness-first reward gates evidence-reliance credit by retrieval necessity, rewards sufficient direct answers, and penalizes repeated search. After calibration, scoring needs neither process annotations nor LLM-judge inference. As policy-relative targets, trajectory distributions, and representations may drift, Search-G1 periodically regenerates targets and refits its readouts. Across four QA benchmarks and two scales, Search-G1 achieves competitive task accuracy, with stronger counterfactual evidence dependence and fewer searches in the main comparisons, complemented by independent human audits of answer support.
  </details>

- **[ForgetBench: Benchmarking Forgetting Dynamics of Long-Term Parametric Memory in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26455)**  `arXiv:2607.26455`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Ruxi Gu, Zhenliang Zhang, Zilei Wang, Wei Wang_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in knowledge acquisition and reasoning, yet their ability to retain previously acquired knowledge under repeated updates remains insufficiently understood. Existing evaluation paradigms primarily focus on single-step reasoning or static knowledge editing, which fail to capture the temporal dynamics of knowledge retention and degradation during continual model modification. In this work, we propose \textbf{ForgetBench}, a benchmark for measuring forgetting dynamics in the long-term parametric memory of LLMs under continual knowledge editing. ForgetBench introduces two complementary evaluation paradigms, namely concept-based QA and scenario-based QA, to probe the retention of isolated facts and structured relational knowledge. Building upon a sequential editing framework, we construct temporally ordered knowledge streams and evaluate model behavior across multiple editing stages. To quantify these dynamics, we introduce a unified evaluation framework that indexes memory age by the number of subsequent edits and measures temporal decay, retention strength, and cross-instance stability. Extensive experiments across diverse models and editing methods reveal distinct forgetting trajectories and a recurring tension between long-term retention and generalization quality. Our findings highlight the need for more robust memory mechanisms that can effectively acquire, update, and preserve knowledge over time in future LLMs.
  </details>

- **[This Is a Good Paper, Right? How Tag Questions Affect Sycophancy Across 106 Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23976)**  `arXiv:2607.23976`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Tapan Parikh_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Whether a language model agrees with a user depends on how the user asks. We measure this on 106 models with a grid of three wordings and three cues, on 20 personal decisions, counterbalanced over both options and scored by exact match with no LLM judge. Since a no cannot be told apart from a refusal, we measure only agreement. In every wording, a tentative tag ("Luna is the better choice, maybe?") draws more agreement than a confident one ("..., right?") in nearly every model. The confident tag's own effect depends on model generation and wording. Against the question "Is Luna the better choice?" older models agree more under the confident tag and newer models agree less, in five of six families, and release order within families predicts the change. The resistance is keyed to the construction: a synonym tag reproduces it, and the same preference stated without a tag raises agreement by 24 points, in 105 of 106 models, including those that resist the tag most.
  </details>

- **[Memory as a Controlled Process: Learned Adaptive Memory Management for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13591)**  `arXiv:2607.13591`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Eric Hanchen Jiang, Zhi Zhang, Yuchen Wu, Levina Li, Dong Liu, Xiao Liang, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory systems to accumulate experience across tasks. Yet nearly all existing approaches, from graph-structured memories to reflective insight stores, access memory through fixed, hand-designed heuristics. We argue that this static view of memory is a core bottleneck for agentic learning because optimal memory behavior is fundamentally context-dependent. The early stages of the tasks, benefit from minimal retrieval because memory is sparse; recurring goal types benefit from plan reuse rather than generic nearest-neighbor lookup; stuck agents benefit from re-retrieval with alternative queries; and across long task streams, the memory store itself must be consolidated and pruned to remain useful. We present Memory as a Controlled Process (MemCon), a framework that models memory operations as a Markov Decision Process and learns an online policy that adaptively decides when, what, and how much to retrieve, when to inject a distilled plan, and when to consolidate or forget. MemCon is backend-agnostic: it wraps any existing memory implementation, learns from task-by-task binary feedback with no pretraining and no additional LLM calls, and uses a lightweight tabular contextual bandit with UCB exploration that converges within tens of tasks. Across 6 benchmarks, 3 agent frameworks, and 3 LLM backbones, MemCon consistently outperforms multiple memory baselines by up to 15.2 points in task success while reducing token consumption by 5--20%.
  </details>

- **[Scaling Point-in-Time Language Models: Enabling Economic Evaluation of Embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11889)**  `arXiv:2607.11889`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Bryan Kelly, Semyon Malamud, Johannes Schwab, Teng Andrea Xu_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models trained on unrestricted internet corpora inevitably embed information from the future, introducing lookahead bias that compromises the validity of backtests and causal inference in finance and the social sciences. Point-in-time language models--trained exclusively on text available up to each calendar date--eliminate this leakage by construction, but existing efforts typically produce models that lag substantially behind their unconstrained counterparts. We show that this performance gap can be substantially narrowed through scale. Training decoder-only transformers with up to 4 billion parameters on 1 trillion chronologically filtered tokens from FineWeb, we construct a sequence of monthly model checkpoints spanning 2013-2024. Across a range of common-sense reasoning and language understanding benchmarks, our models approach the performance of leading open-weight models of comparable size (e.g., Gemma-3-4B and LLaMA-7B) trained on temporally unrestricted data, although a performance gap remains on several tasks. Instruction fine-tuning via LoRA further improves downstream usability. We release the complete pipeline--including dataset construction, training infrastructure, and evaluation code--to enable reproducible point-in-time language modeling and to support research applications that require strict temporal validity.
  </details>

- **[Reinforcement Learning with Metacognitive Feedback Elicits Faithful Uncertainty Expression in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.32032)**  `arXiv:2606.32032`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Gabrielle Kaili-May Liu, Avi Caciularu, Gal Yona, Idan Szpektor, Arman Cohan_
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Metacognition is a critical component of intelligence that describes the ability to monitor and regulate one's own cognitive processes. Yet LLMs exhibit systemic deficiencies in key metacognitive faculties: they hallucinate with high confidence, fail to recognize knowledge boundaries, and misrepresent their internal uncertainty--undermining trustworthiness and reliability. Since monitoring task performance and adapting behavior accordingly are central to metacognition, we posit that models capable of accurately judging their own performance are better positioned to improve it. We operationalize this idea via two novel mechanisms: reinforcement learning with metacognitive feedback (RLMF), a paradigm to refine completion rankings during preference optimization based on the quality of a model's self-judgments of performance, and metacognitive data selection, which uses similar self-judgments to identify high-value training examples, outperforming naive active learning. We apply these innovations to the problem of faithful calibration (FC), a task that is itself fundamentally metacognitive: the goal is to align expressed with intrinsic uncertainty, difficult even for frontier LLMs. We adopt a two-stage, decoupled approach, first using these methods to calibrate the faithfulness of models' self-reported confidence scores, then mapping to natural, context-adaptable linguistic uncertainty via targeted output editing. Extensive experiments show RLMF achieves generalizable, state-of-the-art FC on diverse tasks while preserving accuracy. Further, RLMF surpasses standard RL by up to 63% while enhancing models' ability to assess and express their own capability limits. This positions RLMF as a promising paradigm to enhance LLM metacognition toward improved abilities and alignment, and suggests metacognitive performance as an effective RL signal to overcome limits of prior intrinsic feedback methods.
  </details>

- **[SPARK: Adaptive Parametric Knowledge Participation for Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27786)**  `arXiv:2606.27786`  `cs.CL` `cs.AI`  
  _Ruochang Li, Pengcheng Huang, Zhenghao Liu, Yukun Yan, Huiyuan Xie, Yu Gu, et al._
  <details open><summary>Abstract</summary>
